It is these multitudinous associations that give life its colour and its poetry. They are the garnerings of the journey, and unlike material gains they are no burden to our backs and no anxiety to our mind. "The true harvest of my life," said Thoreau, "is something as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." It was the summary, the essence, of all his experience. We are like bees foraging in the garden of the world, and hoarding the honey in the hive of memory. And no hoard is like any other hoard that ever was or ever will be. The cuckoo calling over the valley, the blackbird fluting in the low boughs in the evening, the solemn majesty of the Abbey, the life of the streets, the ebb and flow of Father Thames—everything whispers to us some secret that it has for no other ear, and touches a chord of memory that echoes in no other brain. Those deeps within us find only a crude expression in the vehicle of words and actions, and our intercourse with men touches but the surface of ourselves. The rest is "as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." It was one of the most companionable of men, William Morris, who said:

That God has made each one of us as lone As He Himself sits.

That is why, in moments of exaltation, our only refuge is silence, and the world of memory within answers the world of suggestion without.

"And what does the seaweed remind you of?" said one, as I looked up after smelling it. "It reminds me," I said, "of all the seas that wash our shores, and of all the brave sailors who are guarding these seas day and night, while we sit here secure. It reminds me also that I have an article to write, and that its title is 'A Bit of Seaweed.'"

message.content:
The myriad connections we form throughout life infuse our existence with vibrancy and depth. These experiences, collected along our journey, represent a wealth of understanding that adds no burden to our physical selves nor stress to our minds. As Thoreau aptly noted, "The true harvest of my life... is something as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." This encapsulates the very essence of his life’s journey. We resemble bees gathering nectar from the vast garden of existence, storing memories in our minds like honey in a hive. Each collection of memories is unique, never to be replicated. The calls of the cuckoo resonating over the valley, the melodic tunes of the blackbird perched in the evening's low branches, the grand presence of the Abbey, the bustling life along the streets, and the rhythmic flow of Father Thames—all these elements share secrets with us that remain unheard by others, resonating within our personal recollections.

Our inner depths often find only rudimentary expression through words and actions, making our interactions with others merely surface-level connections. The more profound aspects of our being remain elusive, "as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." This sentiment was echoed by the sociable William Morris, who expressed the solitude inherent in our existence: 

"That God has made each one of us as lone As He Himself sits."

In times of heightened emotion, it is often silence that provides solace, allowing the vast world of our memories to interact with the external suggestions that surround us.

In a recent exchange, a friend prompted me with a question about the seaweed I was observing. "And what does the seaweed remind you of?" they asked. I replied, “It brings to mind all the oceans that touch our shores and the courageous sailors who protect these waters around the clock while we enjoy our safety. It also reminds me that I need to write an article titled 'A Bit of Seaweed.'"
